sections.content: Foreclosed homes are one of the most reliable ways to find below-market deals in real estate. Whether you are wholesaling, flipping, or building a rental portfolio, foreclosures give you a built-in equity advantage that is hard to beat. But knowing where to look makes all the difference. If you are still searching the wrong places, you are likely missing out on dozens of deals every month. This guide covers the best websites to find foreclosed homes for investing, how each one works, and what you need to do to turn those listings into closed deals. For a broader view of how foreclosures fit into your deal-finding strategy, check out our [How to Find Motivated Sellers: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/finding-motivated-sellers).
Why Foreclosures Are a Gold Mine for Investors

When a homeowner stops making mortgage payments, the lender eventually takes back the property. This creates a situation where the bank or government agency needs to sell quickly and often below market value. Studies show that foreclosed homes sell for an average of 15% to 30% below comparable properties. For an investor, that discount is your profit margin before you even begin negotiating. The key is finding these properties early, before other buyers bid up the price.

The best deals are not found on the MLS. They are found by the investors willing to look where others are not. Foreclosures are one of the few places where motivated sellers and discounted prices reliably overlap.
The Best Websites to Find Foreclosed Homes for Investing
1. HUD Home Store (hudhomestore.gov)

This is a free government website that lists homes owned by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. HUD homes become available when FHA-insured loans go into default. Investors can bid on these properties, though owner-occupants get priority during the first 30 days. After that, investors can submit offers freely. HUD homes are sold as-is, so always budget for repairs. Search by state, county, or zip code to filter results quickly.
2. Fannie Mae HomePath (homepath.fanniemae.com)

Fannie Mae's HomePath website lists REO (Real Estate Owned) properties that Fannie Mae has acquired through foreclosure. Investors will find a solid selection of single-family homes, condos, and multi-unit properties here. The platform is clean and easy to use. One standout feature is the First Look program, which gives owner-occupants 30 days of exclusive access. After that window closes, investors can make offers. Some HomePath properties also qualify for Fannie Mae's renovation loans, which can be useful for flippers.
3. Freddie Mac HomeSteps (homesteps.com)

Similar to HomePath, HomeSteps is Freddie Mac's platform for selling its foreclosed properties. Listings include photos, property details, and offer submission tools. Freddie Mac properties tend to be well-documented and are sold through licensed real estate agents. If you are new to investing, this is a good starting point because the process is straightforward and well-organized. Listings are searchable by location and price range.
4. Auction.com

Auction.com is one of the largest foreclosure auction platforms in the country and a go-to resource for serious investors. The site lists both pre-foreclosure and bank-owned properties available through online and live auctions. You can browse upcoming auctions by state, property type, and opening bid. One important note: many auction properties are sold without the ability to do a full interior inspection, so you need to know how to estimate repair costs from limited information. Active investor markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) consistently have large inventories on this platform.

Before bidding on any auction property, run your numbers using the free [Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator). Auction wins are binding, so knowing your max allowable offer before you bid can save you from a costly mistake.
5. Xome.com

Xome is another major auction and listing site that focuses heavily on bank-owned and foreclosure properties. It partners with major lenders and servicers to list REO inventory nationwide. Xome allows investors to search by location, property type, and auction date. The site also offers detailed property reports and comparable sales data, which makes it easier to evaluate a deal without visiting in person. Registration is free, and you can set up alerts for new listings in your target area.
6. RealtyTrac (realtytrac.com)

RealtyTrac has been a staple for foreclosure investors for over two decades. The platform lists properties at every stage of the foreclosure process, including pre-foreclosure, auction, and REO. Subscriptions start around $49 per month, but the depth of data you get is significant. You can see loan history, estimated equity, and owner contact information on many listings. This is especially valuable if you want to reach out to homeowners before the foreclosure is finalized.
7. Zillow and Realtor.com Foreclosure Filters

Both Zillow and Realtor.com have built-in filters for foreclosure and bank-owned properties. These are not dedicated foreclosure platforms, but they pull REO listings from the MLS and make them easy to find. If you are already using these sites for market research, it takes about 30 seconds to add a foreclosure filter to your search. The downside is that by the time a property appears here, it has likely been seen by many other buyers. Speed matters when using these platforms.
How to Combine Foreclosure Sites With Other Lead Sources

The investors who win the most deals do not rely on just one source. Foreclosure websites are powerful, but they work even better when combined with other motivated seller strategies. For example, homeowners who are behind on their mortgage are often also behind on property taxes. Combining foreclosure searches with [tax delinquent property lists](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/tax-delinquent-property-list-guide) can help you identify motivated sellers before the foreclosure even becomes public record. Similarly, [probate real estate leads](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/probate-real-estate-leads) often overlap with distressed property situations where owners are eager to sell quickly.

items: Stack your lead sources: Use foreclosure sites alongside tax delinquent lists and probate leads
Set up email alerts on every platform so new listings hit your inbox immediately
Build a relationship with a local title company that can flag upcoming foreclosure auctions
Drive neighborhoods after identifying properties online to assess condition and competition
Always calculate your maximum offer before reaching out to avoid emotional bidding

sections.content: What to Do Once You Find a Foreclosure Deal

Finding the property is only step one. Once you have identified a promising foreclosure, you need to move fast and run your numbers accurately. Start by pulling comparable sales within a half-mile radius sold in the last 90 days. Then estimate your repair costs conservatively. A common mistake new investors make is underestimating rehab costs on foreclosed homes, which are often neglected or vandalized. If you are wholesaling the deal, use the 70% rule as a starting framework, then tighten it based on actual comps and repair bids. If you are newer to investing, our guides on [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) and [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) walk you through the full process step by step.

For pre-foreclosure properties where you can contact the owner directly, consider combining your online research with a driving-for-dollars route in the neighborhood. The [Best Driving for Dollars Apps](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/best-driving-for-dollars-apps) can help you log properties and follow up systematically while you are already in the area.

Speed and preparation win deals in the foreclosure market. Have your financing lined up before you make an offer, whether that is hard money, private money, or cash. Banks and government agencies selling REO properties prefer buyers who can close quickly and without contingencies. If you are submitting an offer on a HUD or Fannie Mae property, a pre-approval letter or proof of funds should be ready to attach before you even click submit.
